title: Treadmill: get the big DC motor and controller out
summary: Pull the 1.5–3 hp permanent-magnet DC motor, its controller, the flywheel, belt, rollers, bearings, incline actuator and steel frame from a treadmill. The motor is one of the best generators a scavenger can find. Two people make the job safe.

steps.text: Unplug it and cut the plug off. On folding models, lower the deck flat and strap or tie it so it can't swing up or down while you work.
steps.warn: A folding deck can drop or spring up. Keep hands out of the hinge and gas strut area.

steps.text: Remove the motor hood at the front: usually 4–8 screws along the sides and front edge. Lift it off.

Find the controller board under the hood. On mains-powered treadmills it holds large capacitors charged from the mains. Wait 5 minutes, then measure DC volts across the largest capacitors. If you see more than about 30 V, discharge them with a resistor tool (see safety_discharge_capacitor) and measure again.
steps.warn: Mains treadmill controllers can hold about 170 V DC (120 V countries) or 340 V DC (230 V countries).

steps.text: Photograph the wiring. Label the two motor wires (often red and black, or marked A+ and A-) and unplug them from the controller.
Slacken the drive belt: loosen the motor mounting bolts or the tension bolt so the motor slides toward the roller, then roll the belt off the pulleys.
Undo the motor mounting bolts (usually 2–4) and lift the motor out with its flywheel. It weighs about 8–15 kg.
steps.warn: Lift with your legs and keep fingers clear of the frame edges when the motor comes free.

steps.text: Leave the flywheel on unless you need it off. On many motors it screws onto a reverse (left-hand) thread: it loosens by turning clockwise. Check before forcing it.
Undo the screws holding the controller board and lift it out whole with its heatsink. Keep its wiring loom.
Remove the incline actuator: support the deck, then pull the pins or bolts at both ends of the actuator. Note the label: many run on mains AC, some on DC.
steps.warn: The deck can drop when the last pin comes out. Prop it first.

steps.text: Loosen the two belt-tension bolts at the back end of the side rails (usually hex keys), slide the running belt off, and unbolt the front and rear rollers. Each roller has a bearing at each end.
Unscrew the deck board from the frame. With a helper, unbolt the side rails and uprights if you want the steel tube.
steps.warn: Treadmills weigh 60–120 kg. Never carry or tip the frame alone.

steps.text: Test the motor before you carry it far: spin the shaft by hand with the meter on DC volts across the two motor wires. A good motor gives a few volts that rise as you spin faster.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **The motor.** A permanent-magnet DC motor rated about 90–180 V and 1.5–3 hp. Spun by wind or water it works as a generator. Divide the rated volts on its label by the rated RPM to get volts per RPM; typical motors give about 1 V per 25–45 RPM, so roughly 400–700 RPM charges a 12 V battery. That makes it one of the easiest generators to build with (see build_treadmill_wind_generator and test_motor). It also makes a good variable-speed motor for a lathe, grinder or saw where mains power exists, run from its own controller.
- **Flywheel.** A heavy pulley with a fan. Keep it on if you will belt-drive the motor; it smooths out gusts.
- **Controller board.** A ready-made mains-to-DC speed controller for the motor, plus a bridge rectifier, power transistors, a heatsink and big capacitors.
- **Rollers and bearings.** Steel rollers with sealed bearings make axles, conveyor rollers and cart wheels.
- **Incline actuator.** A strong screw jack for lifting and pushing.
- **Running belt.** Tough reinforced belt: hinges, gaskets, wear pads, a short conveyor.
- **Deck board.** A large, flat, waxed board: a shelf, a table top or a bench.
- **Frame.** Steel tube for carts, racks and turbine towers.
- **Console.** Small speakers, buttons, wiring. On many models the safety key is a magnet that works a reed switch in the console.

## Variations

- Older and budget machines use a brushed DC motor like the one above. Some newer machines use AC or brushless motors with an inverter board; those need different handling and are less useful as simple generators.
- Folding treadmills use a gas strut to lift the deck; it is under pressure. Leave it intact or release it with care.
- Motor voltage and power are on the motor's label. Higher voltage motors give more volts at low RPM.

## What to leave

- The plastic hood and console shell, unless you need sheet plastic.
- Don't open the motor unless the brushes need replacing (see repair_motor_brushes). The magnets are glued in and hard to remove.
